entry.title: Two Envelopes with a Uniform Prior

link.title: Two Envelopes with a Uniform Prior

entry.content:
Problem.

Let $X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,100)$. Two envelopes contain $X$ dollars and $2X$ dollars. You choose an envelope, and open it to observe its amount. You may then keep it or switch to the other envelope. What strategy maximizes the probability of ending with the larger amount, and what is this probability? Does the same strategy maximize the expected amount received?

Solution.

Write $Y$ for the observed amount and $Z$ for the amount in the other envelope. Let $S$ be the event that the selected envelope is the smaller one, so $Y=X$ and $Z=2X$, and let $L$ be the event that it is the larger one, so $Y=2X$ and $Z=X$. Before observing $Y$, both events have probability $1/2$.

1. Update the probabilities after seeing the amount

If $100<Y<200$, the selected envelope must be the larger one: the smaller amount $X$ never exceeds $100$. Keeping it wins with certainty.

If $0<Y<100$, either envelope could have been selected. The conditional densities are

\[f_{Y\mid S}(y)=\frac1{100},\qquad f_{Y\mid L}(y)=\frac1{200}, \qquad 0<y<100.\]

The second density is smaller because $Y=2X$ spreads the same probability mass over an interval twice as long. Since $Y$ is continuous, we use these densities in Bayes’ formula:

\[\mathbb P(S\mid Y=y) =\frac{\frac12\cdot\frac1{100}} {\frac12\cdot\frac1{100}+\frac12\cdot\frac1{200}} =\frac23, \qquad \mathbb P(L\mid Y=y)=\frac13.\]

Equivalently, observing an amount in a short interval $[y,y+\mathrm{d}y]$ corresponds to an interval of width $\mathrm{d}y$ for $X$ if the smaller envelope was selected, but only width $\mathrm{d}y/2$ if the larger envelope was selected. The two explanations therefore have probability ratio $2:1$.

2. Choose the action with the higher winning probability

For $0<y<100$, switching wins exactly when the selected envelope is the smaller one, with conditional probability $2/3$; keeping wins with probability $1/3$. For $100<y<200$, keeping wins with certainty. Thus an optimal strategy is

\[\boxed{ \text{Switch if }Y\leq100;\qquad \text{keep if }Y>100. }\]

The observation $Y=100$ has probability zero, so the action at this boundary does not affect the overall result. Comparing the two actions at each observed amount establishes optimality; randomizing between them cannot improve the conditional winning probability.

To calculate the overall winning probability, condition on which envelope was initially selected. If we selected $X$, then $Y=X\leq100$ and we always switch to $2X$. If we selected $2X$, we keep the larger envelope exactly when $2X>100$, or $X>50$. Therefore

\[\boxed{ \mathbb P(\text{finish with }2X) =\frac12\cdot1+\frac12\mathbb P(X>50) =\frac12+\frac12\cdot\frac12 =\frac34. }\]

3. Maximize the expected amount

For $0<y<100$, the other envelope contains $2y$ with posterior probability $2/3$ and $y/2$ with probability $1/3$. Hence

\[\mathbb E[Z\mid Y=y] =\frac23(2y)+\frac13\left(\frac y2\right) =\frac32y>y.\]

For $100<y<200$, the other envelope certainly contains $y/2<y$. Thus the same strategy also maximizes expected dollars received.

Let $V$ be the final amount under this strategy. Conditional on initially selecting the smaller envelope, $V=2X$. Conditional on initially selecting the larger envelope, $V=X$ when $X\leq50$ and $V=2X$ when $X>50$. Consequently,

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbb E[V] &=\frac12\mathbb E[2X] +\frac12\left( \int_0^{50}\frac{x}{100}\,\mathrm{d}x +\int_{50}^{100}\frac{2x}{100}\,\mathrm{d}x \right)\\ &=50+\frac12(12.5+75) =\boxed{93.75\text{ dollars}}. \end{aligned}\]

For comparison, always keeping or always switching gives expected amount $\frac12\mathbb E[X]+\frac12\mathbb E[2X]=75$ dollars. Observing the amount and acting on it raises the expectation by $18.75$ dollars.

entry.title: HTH Before HHT – A Pattern Race

link.title: HTH Before HHT – A Pattern Race

entry.content:
Problem.

A fair coin is tossed independently. What is the probability that $HTH$ appears as three consecutive outcomes before $HHT$ does?

Solution.

Let $\tau_{HTH}$ and $\tau_{HHT}$ be the numbers of tosses needed for the first complete occurrences of the respective patterns. Define

\[W:=\{\tau_{HTH}<\tau_{HHT}\}, \qquad p:=\mathbb P(W).\]

Method 1. Restart after an unsuccessful attempt

Ignore any initial tails and wait for the first head. Neither pattern can appear before this head, so the probability of eventually winning from this point is still $p$.

Starting from this first $H$, there are three possibilities:

  • The next toss is $H$, with probability $1/2$. Once the sequence ends in $HH$, every additional head preserves that suffix, and the first subsequent tail completes $HHT$. Thus $HTH$ cannot win along this branch.
  • The next two tosses are $TH$, with probability $1/4$. They complete $HTH$, so we win immediately.
  • The next two tosses are $TT$, with probability $1/4$. The sequence ends in $HTT$, neither target has appeared, and no nonempty suffix is a beginning of either target. We therefore start afresh, with winning probability $p$.

By conditioning on these three possibilities,

\[p=\frac12\cdot0+\frac14\cdot1+\frac14p.\]

Consequently,

\[\boxed{\mathbb P(\tau_{HTH}<\tau_{HHT})=p=\frac13.}\]

Method 2. Conditional probabilities given initial tosses

Use $\mathbb P(W\mid H)$ to mean the probability of $W$ conditional on the first toss being $H$; similarly, $\mathbb P(W\mid HT)$ conditions on the first two tosses being $HT$. These conditions specify the initial prefix of the sequence.

Conditioning on the first toss gives

\[p=\frac12\mathbb P(W\mid H)+\frac12\mathbb P(W\mid T).\]

An initial tail contributes no progress toward either pattern, and subsequent tosses are independent of it. Hence

\[\mathbb P(W\mid T)=p, \qquad \mathbb P(W\mid H)=p.\]

Next, condition on the second toss:

\[\mathbb P(W\mid H) =\frac12\mathbb P(W\mid HH) +\frac12\mathbb P(W\mid HT).\]

As in Method 1, an initial $HH$ guarantees that $HHT$ wins when the first tail arrives, so

\[\mathbb P(W\mid HH)=0.\]

After an initial $HT$, a head wins immediately, while a tail leaves $HTT$ and restarts the race. Therefore

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbb P(W\mid HT) &=\frac12\mathbb P(W\mid HTH) +\frac12\mathbb P(W\mid HTT)\\ &=\frac12+\frac12p. \end{aligned}\]

Combining the equations,

\[p=\frac12\left(\frac12+\frac12p\right) =\frac14+\frac14p,\]

which again yields $p=1/3$.

Remark.

Equal probabilities in a fixed window do not imply equal winning probabilities. Each pattern has probability $1/8$ in any specified block of three tosses. However, the race examines overlapping windows and stops at the first occurrence. The patterns interact differently with their partial matches: reaching $HH$ guarantees an eventual $HHT$ win, whereas reaching $HT$ still allows the race to restart. Thus the race is asymmetric, with

\[\mathbb P(\tau_{HTH}<\tau_{HHT})=\frac13, \qquad \mathbb P(\tau_{HHT}<\tau_{HTH})=\frac23.\]

The related poster HHT Before HTH – A Conditional Waiting Time asks for the expected stopping time conditional on $HHT$ winning. This problem instead asks for the probability that $HTH$ wins. The same prefix transitions support both calculations, but the quantities being computed are different.

entry.title: Gamma Exponential Chi Square and Normal Distributions

link.title: Gamma Exponential Chi Square and Normal Distributions

entry.content:
Exponential and chi-square distributions are special cases of the Gamma family. Normal variables enter through their squares: sums of independent squared standard normals are chi-square. Throughout, $\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\lambda)$ uses shape $\alpha$ and rate $\lambda$:

\[ oxed{\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)=\operatorname{Gamma}(1,\lambda)}, \qquad oxed{\chi^2_ u=\operatorname{Gamma}\!\left( rac{ u}{2}, rac12 ight)}.\]

1. Gamma distribution and its parameters

For $\alpha,\lambda>0$, a random variable $G\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\lambda)$ has density

\[f_G(x)= rac{\lambda^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)} x^{\alpha-1}e^{-\lambda x},\qquad x>0,\]

and zero density for $x<0$. The normalizing constant is the Gamma function:

\[\Gamma(\alpha)=\int_0^\infty u^{\alpha-1}e^{-u}\,du, \qquad \Gamma(\alpha+1)=\alpha\Gamma(\alpha), \qquad \Gamma(1)=1,\quad \Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi.\]

The recurrence follows by integration by parts, so $\Gamma(m)=(m-1)!$ for positive integers $m$. Substituting $u=\lambda x$ verifies that the density integrates to one.

Under the alternative shape–scale convention, the scale is $1/\lambda$, so

\[f_G(x)= rac{\lambda^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)} x^{\alpha-1}e^{-\lambda x}, \qquad \mathbb E[G]= rac{\alpha}{\lambda}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(G)= rac{\alpha}{\lambda^2}.\]

Thus a chi-square variable has rate $1/2$, equivalently scale $2$. The second Gamma parameter must always be identified as a rate or a scale.

For any real $p>-\alpha$, the substitution $u=\lambda x$ gives

\[ egin{aligned} \mathbb E[G^p] &= rac{\lambda^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)} \int_0^\infty x^{\alpha+p-1}e^{-\lambda x}\,dx\ &= rac{\Gamma(\alpha+p)}{\Gamma(\alpha)\lambda^p}. \end{aligned}\]

Taking $p=1,2$ and using the Gamma recurrence yields

\[\mathbb E[G]= rac{\alpha}{\lambda}, \qquad \mathbb E[G^2]= rac{\alpha(\alpha+1)}{\lambda^2}, \qquad oxed{\operatorname{Var}(G)= rac{\alpha}{\lambda^2}}.\]

Its moment generating function (MGF) is

\[ egin{aligned} M_G(t) &= rac{\lambda^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)} \int_0^\infty x^{\alpha-1}e^{-(\lambda-t)x}\,dx\ &=\left( rac{\lambda}{\lambda-t} ight)^\alpha, \qquad t<\lambda. \end{aligned}\]

The shape controls the relative dispersion, $\operatorname{sd}(G)/\mathbb E[G]=1/\sqrt\alpha$; the rate controls the scale.

2. Scaling and independent sums

For $c>0$, changing variables in the density gives

\[f_{cG}(x)= rac1c f_G(x/c) = rac{(\lambda/c)^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)} x^{\alpha-1}e^{-(\lambda/c)x}.\]

Consequently,

\[ oxed{cG\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\lambda/c)}, \qquad \lambda G\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,1), \qquad oxed{2\lambda G\sim\chi^2_{2\alpha}}.\]

If $G_i\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha_i,\lambda)$ are independent and have a common rate, their MGFs multiply:

\[M_{\sum_iG_i}(t) =\prod_i\left( rac{\lambda}{\lambda-t} ight)^{\alpha_i} =\left( rac{\lambda}{\lambda-t} ight)^{\sum_i\alpha_i}.\]

Uniqueness of the MGF therefore gives

\[ oxed{\sum_iG_i\sim\operatorname{Gamma}\!\left(\sum_i\alpha_i,\lambda ight)}.\]

With different rates, this product generally does not have a Gamma MGF. Dependence also invalidates the product argument.

3. Exponential variables and Poisson waiting times

Setting $\alpha=1$ gives $E\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$:

\[f_E(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\quad(x>0), \qquad \mathbb P(E>x)=e^{-\lambda x}\quad(x\ge0), \qquad \mathbb E[E]= rac1\lambda,\quad \operatorname{Var}(E)= rac1{\lambda^2}.\]

Its memoryless property follows directly from the survival function:

\[\mathbb P(E>s+t\mid E>s) = rac{e^{-\lambda(s+t)}}{e^{-\lambda s}} =e^{-\lambda t} =\mathbb P(E>t), \qquad s,t\ge0.\]

For independent $E_1,\ldots,E_m\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$, Gamma additivity gives

\[ oxed{T_m=\sum_{i=1}^mE_i\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(m,\lambda)}, \qquad \mathbb E[T_m]= rac m\lambda, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(T_m)= rac m{\lambda^2}.\]

The Gamma distribution with positive integer shape $m$ is also called an Erlang distribution. In a homogeneous Poisson process $N(t)$ of rate $\lambda$, the interarrival times are independent $\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$ variables, so $T_m$ is the time of the $m$th arrival. Equivalently,

\[\mathbb P(T_m>t) =\mathbb P(N(t)\le m-1) =e^{-\lambda t}\sum_{k=0}^{m-1} rac{(\lambda t)^k}{k!}, \qquad t\ge0.\]

Differentiating the survival function recovers

\[f_{T_m}(t) =- rac{d}{dt}\mathbb P(T_m>t) = rac{\lambda^m}{(m-1)!}t^{m-1}e^{-\lambda t}, \qquad t>0.\]

For noninteger shape, the Gamma density still makes sense, but there is no literal “$\alpha$th arrival” interpretation. Among Gamma distributions, only shape $1$ is memoryless.

4. Normal squares and chi-square distributions

For $Z\sim N(0, 1)$,

\[ oxed{Z^2\sim\chi^2_1=\operatorname{Gamma}(1/2,1/2)}.\]

For independent $Z_1,\ldots,Z_ u\sim N(0,1)$ and integer $ u\ge1$, Gamma additivity gives

\[ oxed{ Q=\sum_{i=1}^{ u}Z_i^2 \sim\chi^2_ u =\operatorname{Gamma}\!\left( rac u2, rac12 ight). }\]

entry.title: A Mathematical Review of Linear Regression

link.title: A Mathematical Review of Linear Regression

entry.content:
1. Model, notation, and assumptions

With $n$ observations and $d$ coefficients, including the intercept, write

\[\mathbf y=X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon, \quad X=[\,\mathbf 1_n\ \ \widetilde X\,]\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}, \quad \boldsymbol\beta= \begin{pmatrix}\beta_0\\\widetilde{\boldsymbol\beta}\end{pmatrix},\]

with $y_i=\beta_0+\widetilde{\mathbf x}_i^{\top}\widetilde{\boldsymbol\beta}+\varepsilon_i$, where the predictor vector $\widetilde{\mathbf x}_i\in\mathbb R^{d-1}$, and the $i$-th row of $\widetilde X$ is $\widetilde{\mathbf x}_i^{\top}$. Unless stated otherwise, assume $\operatorname{rank}(X)=d<n$. Least-squares algebra needs no further assumptions. The classical moment assumptions are

\[\mathbb E[\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X]=\mathbf0, \quad \operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X)=\sigma^2I_n, \quad \sigma^2>0.\]

Exact finite-sample $t$ and $F$ inference uses the stronger Gaussian assumption

\[\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X\sim N(\mathbf0,\sigma^2I_n).\]

2. OLS and projection geometry

Ordinary least squares (OLS) minimizes $Q(\mathbf b)=|\mathbf y-X\mathbf b|_2^2$. Its first-order condition gives

\[\nabla Q(\mathbf b)=-2X^{\top}\mathbf y+2X^{\top}X\mathbf b.\]

Hence, as $X$ has full column rank and $X^\top X \succ 0$, we have

\[\boxed{\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}\mathbf y},\]

Denote $H=X(X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}$, then we have $\widehat{\mathbf y}=H\mathbf y$, and residual $\mathbf e=(I_n-H)\mathbf y$. Here, $H$ is the orthogonal projection matrix onto the column space $\mathcal C(X)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. The residual lies in $\mathcal C(X)^\perp=\ker(X^{\top})$, i.e., $X^{\top}\mathbf e=\mathbf0$. The Pythagorean identity gives both the minimization property and a useful expansion:

\[Q(\mathbf b) =\underbrace{\|\mathbf e\|^2}_{\mathrm{SSE}} +(\mathbf b-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})^{\top} X^{\top}X(\mathbf b-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}).\]

3. The intercept, sums of squares, and $R^2$

The intercept FOC gives

\[0=\left.\frac{\partial Q}{\partial\beta_0}\right|_{\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}} =-2\sum_{i=1}^n \left(y_i-\widehat\beta_0-\widetilde{\mathbf x}_i^{\top}\widehat{\widetilde{\boldsymbol\beta}}\right) =-2\sum_{i=1}^n e_i.\]

Consequently, $\sum_i e_i=0$. Define SSE (Sum of Squared Errors), TSS (Total Sum of Squares), and SSR (Regression Sum of Squares) by

\[\mathrm{SSE}=\sum_i(y_i-\widehat y_i)^2, \quad \mathrm{TSS}=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2, \quad \mathrm{SSR}=\sum_i(\widehat y_i-\bar y)^2.\]

Since $\widehat{\mathbf y}-\bar y\mathbf1_n\in\mathcal C(X)$ and $\mathbf e\perp\mathcal C(X)$,

\[\mathbf y-\bar y\mathbf1_n =(\widehat{\mathbf y}-\bar y\mathbf1_n)+\mathbf e \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{\mathrm{TSS}=\mathrm{SSR}+\mathrm{SSE}}.\]

Define

\[R^2=1-\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{\mathrm{TSS}} =\frac{\mathrm{SSR}}{\mathrm{TSS}}.\]

4. Sampling covariance and residual degrees of freedom

Substitution of the model yields

\[\begin{aligned} \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\boldsymbol\beta &=(X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}\boldsymbol\varepsilon,\\ \mathbb E[\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid X]&=\boldsymbol\beta,\\ \operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid X) &=(X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}(\sigma^2I_n)X(X^{\top}X)^{-1} =\sigma^2(X^{\top}X)^{-1}. \end{aligned}\]

The residual satisfies

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbf e =\mathbf y-\widehat{\mathbf y} =(I_n-H)\mathbf y =(I_n-H)X\boldsymbol\beta+(I_n-H)\boldsymbol\varepsilon =(I_n-H)\boldsymbol\varepsilon, \end{aligned}\]

which yields

\[\mathbb E[\mathrm{SSE}\mid X] =\mathbb E[\boldsymbol\varepsilon^{\top}(I_n-H)\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X] =\sigma^2(n-d).\]

Thus fitting a $d$-dimensional mean leaves $n-d$ residual degrees of freedom. Then, the estimator of $\sigma^2$ is given by

\[\boxed{\widehat{\sigma}^2=\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{n-d}}.\]

Under the moment assumptions, OLS is also the best linear unbiased estimator (Gauss–Markov).

5. Gaussian independence and coefficient inference

5.1 Two independence lemmas

Let $\mathbf W\sim N_m(\boldsymbol\mu,\Sigma)$ with $\Sigma \succ 0$.

Lemma 1 (linear and quadratic forms). If $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ is symmetric and $B\in\mathbb R^{k\times m}$, then

\[\boxed{ B\mathbf W\ \perp\!\!\!\perp\ \mathbf W^{\top}A\mathbf W \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad B\Sigma A=0. }\]

Lemma 2 (two quadratic forms, Craig’s theorem). If $A,B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ are symmetric, then

\[\boxed{ \mathbf W^{\top}A\mathbf W\ \perp\!\!\!\perp\ \mathbf W^{\top}B\mathbf W \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A\Sigma B=0. }\]

If $\Sigma=\sigma^2I_m$ and $A$ is an orthogonal projection of rank $r$, then

\[\frac{\mathbf W^{\top}A\mathbf W}{\sigma^2} \sim\chi^2(r,s), \quad s=\frac{\boldsymbol\mu^{\top}A\boldsymbol\mu}{\sigma^2} =\frac{\|A\boldsymbol\mu\|^2}{\sigma^2}.\]

This is the central $\chi^2(r)$ distribution when $A\boldsymbol\mu=0$.

5.2 Applying Lemma 1 to coefficient tests

Under Gaussian errors, conditional on $X$, with $\Sigma=\sigma^2I_n$,

\[\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\sim N(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2(X^{\top}X)^{-1}), \quad \frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2(n-d).\]

Note that $\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top} \mathbf y$ and $\mathrm{SSE} = \mathbf y^{\top}(I_n-H)\mathbf y$, together with

\[\bigl[(X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}\bigr]\Sigma(I_n-H) =\sigma^2(X^{\top}X)^{-1}\bigl[X^{\top}-X^{\top}H\bigr]=0.\]

Thus Lemma 1 and $\widehat{\sigma}^2=\mathrm{SSE}/(n-d)$ give $\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \perp!!!\perp\ \mathrm{SSE}$ and $\widehat\beta_j\ \perp!!!\perp\ \widehat{\sigma}^2$. Under $H_0:\beta_j=0$, we have

\[\boxed{t_j=\frac{\widehat\beta_j}{\widehat{\sigma}\sqrt{\bigl[(X^{\top}X)^{-1}\bigr]_{jj}}}\sim t(n-d)\quad\text{under }H_0}.\]

6. Testing every coefficient versus testing every slope

Let $J=\mathbf1_n\mathbf1_n^{\top}/n$. We have

\[\mathrm{SSR}=\mathbf y^{\top}(H-J)\mathbf y, \quad \mathrm{SSE}=\mathbf y^{\top}(I_n-H)\mathbf y.\]

By $(H-J)(I_n-H)=0.$, Lemma 2 gives

\[\boxed{\mathrm{SSR}\ \perp\!\!\!\perp\ \mathrm{SSE}}.\]

Similarly, by Lemma 2 and $H(I_n-H)=0$,

\[\|\widehat{\mathbf y}\|^2=\mathbf y^{\top}H\mathbf y \ \perp\!\!\!\perp\ \mathrm{SSE}.\]

Under Gaussian errors and $H_0:\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf0$ (including the intercept), $\mathbf y=\boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim N(\mathbf0,\sigma^2I_n)$ conditional on $X$. Since $H$ and $I_n-H$ are projections of ranks $d$ and $n-d$,

\[\frac{\|\widehat{\mathbf y}\|^2}{\sigma^2} =\frac{\mathbf y^{\top}H\mathbf y}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2(d), \quad \frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2(n-d).\]

These quadratic forms are independent, as shown above. Dividing each by its degrees of freedom gives

\[\begin{aligned} F_{\mathrm{all}} &=\frac{\bigl(\|\widehat{\mathbf y}\|^2/\sigma^2\bigr)/d} {\bigl(\mathrm{SSE}/\sigma^2\bigr)/(n-d)}\\ &=\frac{\|\widehat{\mathbf y}\|^2}{d\,\widehat{\sigma}^2} =\frac{\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}^{\top}X^{\top}X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}}{d\,\widehat{\sigma}^2} \sim F_{d,n-d}\quad\text{under }H_0. \end{aligned}\]

As for $H_0:\widetilde{\boldsymbol\beta}=\mathbf0$, with $d\ge2$, $(H-J)X\boldsymbol\beta=(H-J)\beta_0\mathbf1_n=0$. Since $H-J$ has rank $d-1$, $\mathrm{SSR}/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(d-1)$. The restricted fit is $\bar y\mathbf1_n$, with residual sum of squares $\mathrm{TSS}$. Thus

\[\boxed{ F_{\mathrm{slopes}} =\frac{\mathrm{SSR}/(d-1)}{\mathrm{SSE}/(n-d)} =\frac{R^2/(d-1)}{(1-R^2)/(n-d)} \sim F_{d-1,n-d}\quad\text{under }H_0. }\]

The distinction is $|\widehat{\mathbf y}|^2=\mathrm{SSR}+n\bar y^2$: the full-vector test also includes the fitted mean level.

7. Rank deficiency, pseudoinverses, and estimability

Let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ have rank $r<d$, allowing $d\ge n$. Then $X^{\top}X$ is singular, but least squares still has minimizers.

7.1 Definition of the generalized inverse

A generalized inverse $G\in\mathbb R^{d\times n}$ satisfies $XGX=X$ and need not be unique. Here $X^+$ denotes the unique Moore–Penrose inverse, characterized by

\[\begin{gathered} XX^+X=X,\qquad X^+XX^+=X^+,\\ (XX^+)^{\top}=XX^+,\qquad (X^+X)^{\top}=X^+X. \end{gathered}\]

7.2 Properties of the Moore–Penrose inverse

The Moore–Penrose inverse satisfies

\[X^{\top}(I_n-XX^+)=0, \qquad X^+\mathbf y\in\mathcal C(X^{\top})=\ker(X)^\perp.\]

A useful identity is $(X^{\top}X)^+=X^+(X^+)^{\top}$. Together with the defining equations, it gives

\[\begin{aligned} (X^{\top}X)^+X^{\top} &=X^+(X^+)^{\top}X^{\top}=X^+(XX^+)^{\top} =X^+XX^+ =X^+. \end{aligned}\]

For full column rank, this reduces to $X^+=(X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}$.

7.3 Estimation when $X$ is not of full column rank

The Moore–Penrose estimate is

\[\boxed{\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\min} =X^+\mathbf y=(X^{\top}X)^+X^{\top}\mathbf y},\]

which solves the normal equations. Since $\ker(X^{\top}X)=\ker(X)$, all OLS solutions are

\[\boxed{\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=X^+\mathbf y+\mathbf h, \qquad \mathbf h\in\ker(X)}.\]

By $X^+\mathbf y\perp\ker(X)$,

\[\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\|^2 =\|X^+\mathbf y\|^2+\|\mathbf h\|^2 \ge\|X^+\mathbf y\|^2,\]

with equality only for $\mathbf h=\mathbf0$. Thus $\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\min}$ is the unique OLS solution of minimum Euclidean norm. Every OLS solution has the same fitted values and residuals:

\[\widehat{\mathbf y}=XX^+\mathbf y,\qquad \mathbf e=(I_n-XX^+)\mathbf y,\qquad \mathrm{SSE}=\|\mathbf e\|^2.\]

Under the classical moment assumptions,

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbb E[\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\min}\mid X] &=X^+X\boldsymbol\beta,\\ \operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\min}\mid X) &=\sigma^2X^+(X^+)^{\top}=\sigma^2(X^{\top}X)^+. \end{aligned}\]

Hence $\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\min}$ is unbiased for the row-space component of $\boldsymbol\beta$; it is unbiased for $\boldsymbol\beta$ itself exactly when $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathcal C(X^{\top})$. Since $I_n-XX^+$ has rank $n-r$,

\[\mathbb E[\mathrm{SSE}\mid X] =\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}(I_n-XX^+)=\sigma^2(n-r), \qquad \boxed{\widehat{\sigma}^2=\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{n-r}}\quad(n>r).\]

The residual degrees of freedom are $n-r$. If $r=n$, this variance estimate is unavailable.

7.4 Which quantities are estimable?

A linear functional $L=\mathbf a^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta$ is estimable if some linear estimator $\mathbf u^{\top}\mathbf y$ is unbiased. The criterion is

\[\boxed{ \mathbf a^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta\text{ is estimable} \iff \mathbf a\perp\ker(X) \iff \mathbf a\in\mathcal C(X^{\top}). }\]

Indeed, $\mathbb E[\mathbf u^{\top}\mathbf y\mid X]=\mathbf u^{\top}X\boldsymbol\beta$ equals $\mathbf a^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta$ for every $\boldsymbol\beta$ exactly when $X^{\top}\mathbf u=\mathbf a$. Equivalently, the value of $L$ must be unchanged when any $\mathbf h\in\ker(X)$ is added to $\boldsymbol\beta$.

For estimable $\mathbf a$, every OLS solution gives the same estimate because $\mathbf a^{\top}\mathbf h=0$. In particular,

\[\begin{gathered} \widehat L=\mathbf a^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\min}, \quad \mathbb E[\widehat L\mid X]=L,\\ \operatorname{Var}(\widehat L\mid X)=\sigma^2\mathbf a^{\top}(X^{\top}X)^+\mathbf a, \quad \widehat{\operatorname{se}}(\widehat L) =\widehat{\sigma}\sqrt{\mathbf a^{\top}(X^{\top}X)^+\mathbf a}. \end{gathered}\]

The exact test of $H_0:L=L_0$ is

\[\boxed{ t=\frac{\widehat L-L_0} {\widehat{\sigma}\sqrt{\mathbf a^{\top}(X^{\top}X)^+\mathbf a}} \sim t(n-r)\quad\text{under }H_0. }\]

The independence follows from Lemma 1 and

\[\left(\mathbf a^{\top}X^+\right)\Sigma \left(I_n-XX^+\right) =\sigma^2\mathbf a^{\top}(X^+-X^+XX^+)=0.\]

Hence $\widehat L\perp!!!\perp\mathrm{SSE}$. The residual projection has rank $n-r$ and $\mathrm{SSE}/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n-r)$.

7.5 Example: a duplicated block of predictors

Let $Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ satisfy $\operatorname{rank}([\,\mathbf1_n\ Z\,])=p+1$, and set $X=[\,\mathbf1_n\ Z\ Z\,]\in\mathbb R^{n\times(2p+1)}$. For coefficient blocks $\boldsymbol\beta_1,\boldsymbol\beta_2\in\mathbb R^p$,

\[\boldsymbol\beta= \begin{pmatrix}\beta_0\\\boldsymbol\beta_1\\\boldsymbol\beta_2\end{pmatrix}, \qquad X\boldsymbol\beta=\beta_0\mathbf1_n+Z(\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2).\]

Let $(\widehat\alpha,\widehat{\mathbf b})$ be the unique OLS fit of the reduced model:

\[(\widehat\alpha,\widehat{\mathbf b}) =\underset{\alpha\in\mathbb R,\,\mathbf b\in\mathbb R^p}{\operatorname{argmin}} \|\mathbf y-\alpha\mathbf1_n-Z\mathbf b\|^2.\]

Since $\ker(X)={(0,\mathbf c^{\top},-\mathbf c^{\top})^{\top}:\mathbf c\in\mathbb R^p}$, all OLS solutions and the minimum-norm choice are

\[\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta} =\begin{pmatrix}\widehat\alpha\\\widehat{\mathbf b}/2+\mathbf c\\\widehat{\mathbf b}/2-\mathbf c\end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf c\in\mathbb R^p, \qquad \boxed{\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\min} =\begin{pmatrix}\widehat\alpha\\\widehat{\mathbf b}/2\\\widehat{\mathbf b}/2\end{pmatrix}}.\]

The equal split follows from

\[\|\widehat{\mathbf b}/2+\mathbf c\|^2 +\|\widehat{\mathbf b}/2-\mathbf c\|^2 =\tfrac12\|\widehat{\mathbf b}\|^2+2\|\mathbf c\|^2.\]

The intercept $\beta_0$ and block sum $\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2$ are estimable; the individual blocks are not. The equal split is a minimum-norm convention. Here $r=p+1$, so $\widehat{\sigma}^2=\mathrm{SSE}/(n-p-1)$ when $n>p+1$.

8. Regularization

Ridge and lasso change the optimization problem by penalizing coefficients. With an unpenalized intercept and $D=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,\ldots,1)$, ridge solves

\[\min_{\mathbf b}\left\{\|\mathbf y-X\mathbf b\|^2+\lambda\mathbf b^{\top}D\mathbf b\right\}, \quad \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\lambda} =(X^{\top}X+\lambda D)^{-1}X^{\top}\mathbf y, \quad \lambda>0.\]
Penalizing all slopes makes this inverse well defined even when predictor columns are linearly dependent. Ridge trades bias for reduced variance; its fitted-value matrix is generally not an orthogonal projection. Lasso replaces the quadratic penalty by $\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{d-1} b_j $, which can set slopes exactly to zero and can have nonunique coefficients under collinearity. Penalties depend on predictor scales, so standardization and the convention for $\lambda$ matter.
entry.summary: Least squares, projection geometry, inference, and estimability

entry.title: A Conditional Expectation for Normal Variables

link.title: A Conditional Expectation for Normal Variables

entry.content:
Problem.

$X$ and $Y$ are jointly normal, and each has distribution $N(0,1)$, with correlation $\rho \in (-1, 1)$. What is $\mathbb E[X\mid X+Y>0]$?

Solution.

Let $S=X+Y$. Then $S\sim N(0,\sigma_S^2)$, where $\sigma_S^2=2(1+\rho)>0$. The joint law is symmetric in $X$ and $Y$, so $\mathbb E[X\mid S]=\mathbb E[Y\mid S]$ and

\[\boxed{\mathbb E[X\mid S] =\frac12\mathbb E[X+Y\mid S] =\frac S2.}\]

Since $\mathbb P(S>0)=1/2$ and $\mathbf1_{{S>0}}$ is a function of $S$, the tower property gives

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbb E[X\mid S>0] &=\frac{\mathbb E[X\mathbf1_{\{S>0\}}]}{\mathbb P(S>0)}\\ &=2\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[X\mathbf1_{\{S>0\}}\mid S]\right]\\ &=2\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[X\mid S]\mathbf1_{\{S>0\}}\right]\\ &=2\mathbb E\!\left[\frac S2\mathbf1_{\{S>0\}}\right]\\ &=\mathbb E[S\mathbf1_{\{S>0\}}]\\ &=\frac{1}{\sigma_S\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_0^\infty s e^{-s^2/(2\sigma_S^2)}\,ds\\ &=\frac{\sigma_S}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \left[-e^{-s^2/(2\sigma_S^2)}\right]_0^\infty\\ &=\frac{\sigma_S}{\sqrt{2\pi}} =\boxed{\sqrt{\frac{1+\rho}{\pi}}}. \end{aligned}\]

entry.title: Traffic Clumps and Record Minima
entry.content:
Problem.

You have N cars that are all traveling in the same direction on an infinitely long one-lane highway. Unfortunately, they are all going at different speeds and cannot pass each other. Eventually, the cars will clump up in one or more traffic jams. In terms of N, what is the expected number of clumps of cars?

Solution.

1. Clumps correspond to record minima

Index the cars from front to back, with distinct desired speeds $v_1,\ldots,v_N$. Assume finite initial gaps and a uniformly random ordering of the speeds; i.i.d. continuous speeds also satisfy the ordering assumption. Each car keeps its desired speed until it catches a slower clump, whose speed it then adopts.

Let $C_N$ be the eventual number of clumps, and define

\[m_0=+\infty, \qquad m_i=\min_{1\leq j\leq i}v_j.\]

Inductively, the rearmost clump among the first $i-1$ cars eventually travels at speed $m_{i-1}$. If $v_i<m_{i-1}$, car $i$ cannot catch any clump ahead and starts a new clump. If $v_i>m_{i-1}$, its positive relative speed and the finite gap ensure that it eventually joins the rearmost clump ahead. Hence the clump leaders are exactly the record minima:

\[I_i:=\mathbf1_{\{v_i<m_{i-1}\}}, \qquad I_1=1, \qquad C_N=\sum_{i=1}^N I_i.\]

For the example, read $3,1,4,6,8,2,7,9,5$ from front to back. Its record minima are $3$ and $1$, so there are two clumps: the first car, and a clump led by the car of speed $1$ containing every remaining car.

2. Take expectations

Under a uniformly random ordering, each of the first $i$ positions is equally likely to contain their minimum. Therefore

\[\mathbb P(I_i=1) =\mathbb P\!\left(v_i=\min_{1\leq j\leq i}v_j\right) =\frac1i.\]

Linearity of expectation gives

\[\boxed{ \mathbb E[C_N] =\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb E[I_i] =\sum_{i=1}^N\frac1i =H_N. }\]

No independence assumption between the indicators is needed for this step.

entry.title: An Acute Triangle on a Circle

link.title: An Acute Triangle on a Circle

entry.content:
Problem.

Three points are chosen independently and uniformly on the circumference of a circle. What is the probability that they form an acute triangle?

Solution.

1. Translate the angle condition into a semicircle condition

Let $G_1,G_2,G_3$ be the angular lengths of the arcs between successive sampled points, so $G_1+G_2+G_3=2\pi$. By the inscribed-angle theorem, the triangle’s angles are $G_1/2,G_2/2,G_3/2$, in the corresponding opposite order. Hence

\[\text{the triangle is acute} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \max\{G_1,G_2,G_3\}<\pi.\]

A gap greater than $\pi$ leaves all three points on a complementary arc shorter than $\pi$, and conversely. Thus the triangle is obtuse exactly when its vertices lie in some open semicircle.

Coincident points and antipodal pairs have probability zero. Right triangles therefore have probability zero, and the acute-triangle probability is the complement of the semicircle probability.

2. Anchor the semicircle at a sampled point

Label the original sampled points $P_1,P_2,P_3$. For each $i$, let $A_i$ be the event that both other points lie in the clockwise open semicircle beginning at $P_i$. Conditional on $P_i$, each of the two other points independently falls in that semicircle with probability $1/2$. Hence

\[\mathbb P(A_i)=\left(\frac12\right)^2=\frac14.\]

If the points fit in an open semicircle, its first sampled point in clockwise order is an anchor for which $A_i$ holds. Conversely, each $A_i$ puts all three points in some open semicircle. Thus the semicircle event is $A_1\cup A_2\cup A_3$.

The events $A_i$ are pairwise disjoint. If both $A_i$ and $A_j$ held, the clockwise angular distance from $P_i$ to $P_j$ and the clockwise distance back from $P_j$ to $P_i$ would both be less than $\pi$. This is impossible because they sum to $2\pi$.

Consequently, the semicircle event has probability $\sum_{i=1}^3\mathbb P(A_i)=3/4$, and

\[\boxed{\mathbb P(\text{acute})=1-\frac34=\frac14.}\]

Related post. All Points in a Semicircle gives the general probability $N/2^{N-1}$ for $N$ independent uniform points. This problem uses its $N=3$ case and takes the complement.

entry.title: Three People at a Round Table

link.title: Three People at a Round Table

entry.content:
Problem.

Three people choose three distinct seats uniformly at random around a circular table with eight seats. What is the probability that at least two of them sit next to each other?

Solution.

Number the seats $1,\ldots,8$ clockwise, with seats $8$ and $1$ adjacent. There are $\binom83=56$ equally likely sets of three occupied seats, since each set allows the same $3!$ assignments of people. Let $N$ be the number of these sets with no adjacent occupied seats. The required probability is $1-N/56$.

To count $N$, temporarily mark one occupied seat as the starting point. Reading clockwise from it, let $g_1,g_2,g_3$ be the numbers of empty seats between successive occupied seats, including the gap back to the start. The five empty seats must form three nonempty gaps:

\[g_1+g_2+g_3=5, \qquad g_i\geq1.\]

Stars and bars gives $\binom{5-1}{3-1}=\binom42=6$ ordered gap triples. There are $8$ choices for the starting seat, and each starting seat and gap triple determines a configuration. This gives $8\binom42$ configurations with a marked starting seat.

Each occupied-seat set is counted exactly $3$ times, because any of its three occupied seats can be marked as the start. For example, the set ${1,3,5}$ is counted once starting at $1$, once at $3$, and once at $5$. Therefore,

\[N=\frac{8\binom42}{3}=16.\]

Taking the complement,

\[\boxed{ \mathbb P(\text{at least one adjacent pair}) =1-\frac{16}{56} =\frac57. }\]

Related post. The positive-gap count is an application of Stars and Bars – Empty and Nonempty Groups.

entry.title: Ants on a String
entry.content:
Problem.

500 ants are randomly put on a 1-foot string (independent uniform distribution for each ant between 0 and 1). Each ant randomly moves toward one end of the string (equal probability to the left or right) at constant speed of 1 foot/minute until it falls off at one end of the string. Also assume that the size of the ant is infinitely small. When two ants collide head-on, they both immediately change directions and keep on moving at 1 foot/min. What is the expected time for all ants to fall off the string?

Solution.

The key observation is that a collision is equivalent to exchanging labels. If we swap the two ants’ labels whenever they collide and reverse direction, each label continues moving in its original direction. The occupied positions and all departure times are unchanged. Thus, we may calculate the time until the string is empty by letting the ants pass straight through one another.

In this equivalent model, let $X_i\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]$ be the initial position of ant $i$. Its departure time, measured in minutes, is

\[T_i= \begin{cases} X_i,&\text{if it initially moves left},\\ 1-X_i,&\text{if it initially moves right}. \end{cases}\]

For $0\leq t\leq1$,

\[\mathbb P(T_i\leq t) =\frac12\mathbb P(X_i\leq t) +\frac12\mathbb P(X_i\geq1-t) =\frac12t+\frac12t=t.\]

Therefore $T_i\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]$. The initial positions and direction choices are independent across ants, so the departure times in this equivalent model are also independent.

All ants have fallen off when the last one leaves. Hence

\[T=\max_{1\leq i\leq500}T_i, \qquad \mathbb P(T\leq t) =\prod_{i=1}^{500}\mathbb P(T_i\leq t) =t^{500}, \quad 0\leq t\leq1.\]

Using the tail-integral formula for a nonnegative random variable,

\[\boxed{ \mathbb E[T] =\int_0^1\mathbb P(T>t)\,dt =\int_0^1(1-t^{500})\,dt =\frac{500}{501}\text{ minutes}. }\]
